806.title: Rebuild my church
806.hook: at San Damiano a crucifix tells Francis to rebuild; he starts with stones
806.howItsDone: The San Damiano cross is kept in the Basilica of Saint Clare in Assisi, and copies of it hang in Franciscan churches and homes; pilgrims pray before it and visit the restored church of San Damiano.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis: a man who crossed the lines unarmed. Your line was across the lines. Today we step back, before Damietta, to how Francis started. Day eight hundred six.

A small church outside the walls of Assisi, and it's falling down. Cracked walls, a sagging roof, a priest too poor to fix any of it. Inside hangs a painted cross, Christ stretched on it with his eyes wide open. A young man, the son of a rich cloth merchant, comes in to pray. He's restless, unsure what his life is for. He kneels in front of that cross. And, the early lives of Francis say, the cross speaks. Today's word is the place: San Damiano.
screen: `A CHURCH FALLING DOWN.` → `A PAINTED CROSS, EYES OPEN.` → `THE CROSS SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Start with the words. The church was San Damiano. Bonaventure, in his life of Francis, gives the voice from the cross like this: Francis, go and repair my house, which, as you see, is falling into ruin. Next, how Francis heard it. He took it literally. The roof was falling in, so he would fix the roof. He sold cloth from his father's shop, and a horse, and brought the money to the priest. The priest, afraid of Francis's father, wouldn't take it, and Francis tossed it onto a windowsill as if it were dust. Then, the stones. With no money to spend, he begged for building stones in the streets of Assisi, where everyone knew him as a merchant's son. Some people mocked him. He carried stones on his own back, set them with his own hands, and the little church stood again. He went on to repair other chapels the same way. Finally, the larger meaning. Bonaventure writes that Francis came to see, only later, that the words were mainly about the Church itself, the Church Christ bought with his own blood. Saint Paul says the same about people, in the Douay-Rheims, writing to a quarreling congregation: "you are God's building." The brothers who gathered around Francis would carry his way far beyond Assisi. But it started with a young man doing the job right in front of him, literally, one stone at a time. That's today's line: start with stones.
screen: `GO AND REPAIR MY HOUSE.` · `HE TOOK IT LITERALLY.` · `BEGGING FOR STONES IN ASSISI.` · `THE CHURCH IS PEOPLE TOO.` · then, large: `START WITH STONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repair one small thing. For the sit, find one small broken thing in your life: a loose button, a squeaky hinge, a strained friendship, a promise you let slide. Choose one you could actually fix today, not the biggest one. Hold it in mind, and plan the first stone: the needle, the screwdriver, the message you'll send. If you pray, you can hold the words from the cross: go and repair my house. After the bell, set that first stone in place. The bell holds the time.
San Damiano. The crumbling church outside Assisi whose cross spoke to Francis, who repaired it stone by stone before understanding the words meant the whole Church. Today's word.
Your line: start with stones. Today, when something big needs fixing, find the smallest real piece of it and do that piece with your own hands. Day eight hundred six.

find stones and start fixing this chapel.

what it means: words Francis heard before the cross at San Damiano, and he began by fixing the building, stone by stone.

807.title: The first crib (Greccio, 1223)
807.hook: Francis sets up a manger with an ox and donkey so people can see
807.howItsDone: Catholic families and parishes set up a crib, or nativity scene, for Advent and Christmas; some wait until Christmas Eve to lay the figure of the child in the manger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, San Damiano, and a crucifix that asked Francis to rebuild. Your line was start with stones. What small thing did you put back together? Day eight hundred seven.

A bundle of hay. An ox. A donkey. A rough wooden feeding trough in a hillside village called Greccio, in the middle of a winter night. People climb up from the farms around with candles and torches, and the woods fill with light and singing. In Celano's telling no one lays a baby in the straw. There's a manger, two animals breathing in the cold, and a small man in a patched habit, overflowing with joy. Francis of Assisi has asked a friend to build this. Today's word is the village: Greccio.
screen: `HAY, AN OX, A DONKEY.` → `TORCHES ON A WINTER NIGHT.` → `AN EMPTY MANGER.`

segments.voice: Start with why. Thomas of Celano, who wrote an early life of Francis, says Francis wanted to see with his own eyes how the child of Bethlehem had lain in a manger, with the hardship of it, the ox and the ass standing by. Francis had heard the Christmas story all his life. He wanted the village to see it, not only hear it. The Gospel line he had in mind is Luke's, which in the Douay-Rheims reads: "and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." Then, the animals. They aren't in Luke. They come from the prophet Isaiah: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." Tradition placed those two animals beside the manger, and Francis put real ones there. A dumb beast, the prophet says, knows where its food comes from. Francis wanted people to stand next to one and remember. Next, the Mass. A priest celebrated Mass right over the manger. Francis, who was a deacon and never a priest, sang the Gospel and then preached, and Celano says he called Jesus the child of Bethlehem, saying the word Bethlehem so tenderly it sounded like a lamb's bleat. Celano adds that one man there saw a child lying in the manger as if asleep, and Francis seemed to wake him. Last, what stayed. Celano doesn't call Greccio the first of anything; first is the title tradition gave it later. What Greccio gave was a habit. Catholic homes and parishes still set out a crib in Advent, with an ox and a donkey nearby. A faith you can stand in front of, and see.
screen: `HE WANTED TO SEE IT WITH HIS EYES.` · `THE OX AND ASS COME FROM ISAIAH.` · `MASS SUNG OVER THE MANGER.` · `A HABIT THAT STAYED.` · then, large: `NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set up something visible for faith, or for whatever you hold dear. It can be small. A crucifix moved to where you'll actually pass it. A holy card on the fridge. A candle on the table. A photograph of someone you pray for, or simply love. Choose it now, and if it's in reach, put it in place. Then sit and look at it, the way the people at Greccio looked at an empty manger. If you pray, you can let the sight of it be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
Greccio. The hillside village where Francis set out a manger with an ox and a donkey so people could see the Christmas story. Today's word.
Your line: so they could see. Today, notice one thing in your home that shows what you love without a word, and keep it where people can see it. Day eight hundred seven.

808.title: The wounds (La Verna, 1224)
808.hook: near the end of his life, Francis receives the marks of the wounds of Christ
808.howItsDone: Franciscans keep a feast of the Stigmata of Saint Francis, and Franciscan friars care for the sanctuary at La Verna, where pilgrims still come to pray at the place of the vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Greccio, an empty manger, an ox and a donkey. Your line was so they could see. What did you put where you'd see it? Day eight hundred eight.

"I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Saint Paul wrote that to the Galatians, near the end of his letter. In another letter he lists beatings and a stoning, and some readers take the marks to be those scars. Marks earned on the road. Now carry that sentence up a wooded mountain in Tuscany called La Verna, where Francis has gone with a few brothers to fast and pray, away from everyone. He is ill and worn out. What happens on that mountain gives Paul's word a new life. Today's word is stigmata.
screen: `I BEAR THE MARKS.` → `A MOUNTAIN CALLED LA VERNA.` → `A WORN-OUT MAN AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: First, the vision. Thomas of Celano and Saint Bonaventure both tell it. While Francis prays, he sees a figure like a seraph, the angel of Isaiah's vision, with six wings, and between the wings a man fixed to a cross. Francis is torn between joy at the beauty of it and grief at the suffering. He doesn't understand what he has seen. Then, the marks. When the vision fades, the accounts say, the signs of nails appear in his hands and feet, and a wound opens in his side. Not paint, not a vision any more, but wounds he has to wrap. Next, the hiding. Francis did not show them off. Celano says he hid them with great care, covering his hands, wearing something on his feet, and only a few close brothers knew while he lived. The marks were not a trophy. They were something given, and he guarded them like a secret between friends. Last, what it means. The Church reads the stigmata not as a magic trick but as love made visible: Francis had spent years trying to follow Christ in poverty and humility, and his body, the tradition says, came to carry the shape of that love. Paul's word for the marks, stigmata, became the Church's word for this. Franciscans keep a feast of the stigmata of Saint Francis, and La Verna is still a place of prayer. Some readers take the accounts as a miracle exactly as told, and some ask what the brothers saw and how they described it. Either way, the story is about a man marked by love.
screen: `A SERAPH, AND A MAN ON A CROSS.` · `NAILS, AND A WOUND IN THE SIDE.` · `HE HID THEM.` · `LOVE MADE VISIBLE.` · then, large: `I BEAR THE MARKS OF THE LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in pain, or, if you don't pray, hold them in mind. Settle, and name one person to yourself: someone sick, grieving, hurting in a way you can see or a way they've only told you about. Picture their hands. Their face. Don't try to fix anything. If you pray, you can simply say their name to God, and stay with it. If you don't, keep them in your attention, gently, for the whole sit, the way you'd sit beside a hospital bed. The bell holds the time.
Stigmata. Paul's word for the marks of Jesus that he bore, and the Church's word for the wounds of Christ that Francis received on La Verna. Today's word.
Your line: marked by love. Today, look at one scar or worn spot you carry, on your body or in your life, and ask what love it came from. Day eight hundred eight.

809.title: Canticle of the Creatures (1225)
809.hook: tradition says he was nearly blind when he sang of brother sun, sister water, and at the end sister death
809.howItsDone: Franciscans sing and pray the Canticle of the Creatures, sometimes called the Canticle of Brother Sun, and its opening words gave the title to a papal letter on care for creation, Laudato si'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, La Verna, and wounds Francis hid with great care. Your line was marked by love. Whose pain did you hold? Day eight hundred nine.

Laudato si', mi' Signore. Four words in the old Italian of Umbria, the everyday speech of Assisi, not the Latin of the Church. Praised be you, my Lord. Tradition says Francis made the song that starts with them near the end of his life, sick, in pain from his eyes, unable to bear the light, lying in a small hut near San Damiano where Clare and her sisters lived. A man who could barely look at the sun wrote a song that names it first among the creatures. And he wanted his brothers to sing it, out loud, as they went about. Today's word is the first creature he named: Brother Sun.
screen: `PRAISED BE YOU, MY LORD.` → `IN THE SPEECH OF ASSISI.` → `A SICK MAN SINGS OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: First, the family. The canticle walks through creation and gives everything a name like a relative. Brother sun, who brings the day and is beautiful and radiant. Sister moon and the stars, bright and precious. Brother wind, and air, and every kind of weather. Sister water, which the song calls useful, humble, precious and pure. Brother fire, who lights the night, playful and strong. And our sister, mother earth, who feeds us and brings out fruit and colored flowers and grass. Nothing in it is just a thing. Everything is kin. Then, the peacemakers. Tradition says a verse was added when the bishop and the mayor of Assisi were feuding: praise for those who forgive for love, and bear sickness and trouble in peace. The brothers sang it in front of both men, the story goes, and the quarrel ended. Next, the last guest. Near the very end comes a line that is hard to sing lightly: praised be you, my Lord, for our sister bodily death, from whom no one living can escape. Not an enemy. Not a thief in the night. A sister. Tradition says Francis added this verse when he knew he was dying, and asked his brothers to sing the canticle to him. Last, the old songbook. The canticle sits beside the psalms the Church already sang: in the Douay-Rheims Psalm 148 calls on sun and moon and stars, fire and hail, snow and ice, mountains and beasts, to praise the Lord. Francis took that old call and made it a family. That late verse is why today's line is sister death.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · `A VERSE FOR THE PEACEMAKERS.` · `OUR SISTER BODILY DEATH.` · `THE PSALM'S OLD CALL, MADE FAMILY.` · then, large: `LAUDATO SI', MI' SIGNORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise one element by name. Pick one that's close right now. The water in a glass. The light through a window. The air going in and out of you. The ground under your chair. Give it its name the way the canticle does: brother, sister. Then just attend to it: how it helps you, how quietly it does its work. If you pray, you can borrow Francis's own opening for it: praised be you, my Lord. If you don't, let gratitude be enough. The bell holds the time.
Brother Sun. The first creature Francis named in his canticle, praising God through sun and moon, wind and water, fire and earth, down to sister death. Today's word.
Your line: sister death. Today, when something ends, a meal, a conversation, the light in the evening, see if you can let it go like family, not like a thief. Day eight hundred nine.

810.title: Clare and the monstrance
810.hook: tradition says Clare held up the Eucharist when soldiers attacked her convent
810.howItsDone: In Catholic churches the consecrated host is placed in a monstrance for adoration and Benediction, and parishes hold hours of Eucharistic adoration when people come to pray before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song of Brother Sun and sister water. Your line was sister death. Did you let something end gently? Day eight hundred ten.

A statue of Clare of Assisi: a woman in a plain habit, holding a gold sunburst on a stand, with a small round window at the center. It's a monstrance, the vessel used to show the consecrated host so people can see it and pray. She holds it up, toward something just out of the frame. Clare was the young woman from Assisi who followed Francis into poverty, and yesterday's song, tradition says, was made in a hut beside the house where she and her sisters lived, San Damiano. So what is just out of the frame? An army. Today's word is her name: Clare.
screen: `A GOLD SUNBURST ON A STAND.` → `HELD UP TOWARD SOMETHING.` → `WHAT'S OUT OF THE FRAME?`

segments.voice: First, the attack. The early Life of Saint Clare tells it. Soldiers serving the emperor, at war in the valley, came to San Damiano, climbed over the walls and got into the cloister. The sisters ran to Clare, terrified. She was sick and could not walk. Then, what she did. She had herself carried to the door, and had the Body of the Lord brought and set in front of her. She lay down before it in prayer, and prayed with the words of a psalm, asking God not to hand over to beasts the souls that confess to him, and to guard her sisters. Next, the voice. The Life says she heard a voice, like a little child's, promising to protect them always. She asked for the city too, and was told the city would suffer but be defended. She turned to the sisters and told them not to be afraid. The soldiers, the story says, scrambled back over the walls and left. Last, the vessel. The Life does not mention a gold monstrance. It speaks of a small box of silver and ivory, where the host was kept. The great sunburst belongs to the statues, not to the Life. So the statues are true to the story's heart, if not to its silverware. Clare didn't wave a weapon or make a speech. She put the Eucharist between her sisters and the danger, and she held it up. The Douay-Rheims psalm puts the idea plainly: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."
screen: `SOLDIERS OVER THE WALL.` · `CARRIED TO THE DOOR, SHE PRAYED.` · `A CHILD'S VOICE: I WILL PROTECT YOU.` · `A SILVER BOX, NOT A GOLD SUNBURST.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your home's protection, or, if you don't pray, hold it in mind with care. Close your eyes and walk through it in your imagination. The front door. The kitchen. The rooms where people sleep. Think of who lives there, or who used to, or who comes and goes. Linger at the door. If you pray, you can use today's psalm: unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it. If you don't, simply wish each room well. The bell holds the time.
Clare. Sick at the door of San Damiano, she held up the Body of the Lord as soldiers came over the wall. Today's word.
Your line: she held it up. Today, when something threatens your peace, notice what you hold up first, and whether it's what you love. Day eight hundred ten.

811.title: Dominic (1170–1221)
811.hook: a Spanish canon starts an order of preachers who live poor and study hard
811.howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters, and lay Dominicans, live a rhythm of prayer, study and preaching, and Dominican friars write O.P. after their names for the Order of Preachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare at the door of San Damiano, with soldiers on the wall. Your line was she held it up. What did you hold up first? Day eight hundred eleven.

A student in a Spanish town is selling his books. In his day a book was handwritten on parchment, slow and costly, and these carry his own notes in the margins. They are the tools of everything he's working toward. But there's a famine, and people in the streets are starving. Jordan of Saxony, who knew him and wrote an early account of him, says he sold the books and gave the money away. A brother remembered him saying he would not study on dead skins while living people died of hunger. His name was Dominic. Years later, the same man who sold his books would found an order built around study. Today's word is his name: Dominic.
screen: `A STUDENT SELLS HIS BOOKS.` → `NOT ON DEAD SKINS.` → `THE SAME MAN BUILDS ON STUDY.`

segments.voice: First, the road. Dominic became a canon, a priest living in community at the cathedral of Osma, and traveled north with his bishop, Diego. In the south of France they found preachers arriving with horses and servants and fine clothes, and being ignored. People there were listening to wandering teachers who lived poor. Diego and Dominic, Jordan says, drew a plain conclusion: if you want to be heard, go on foot, with nothing, the way the apostles went. Then, the order. Dominic gathered a small band of preachers around him, and the Church approved them as a new kind of religious order: not monks staying in one monastery, but friars sent out. They begged for their food, owned little, and went where people were. Jesus's charge at the end of Mark, in the Douay-Rheims, was their whole job description: "Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Next, the books come back. A preacher needs something true to say, so Dominic sent his brothers to study, and study hard, and set them in towns where the schools were. The student who sold his books for the hungry now asked his brothers to fill their heads, so they could feed people another way. Last, the motto. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican himself, later wrote that it is a greater thing to contemplate and pass on to others what you've contemplated than only to contemplate. Dominicans took that as their own. They still sign their names with the letters O.P., for the Order of Preachers. Prayer, then study, then the handing on: to contemplate and to share.
screen: `PREACHERS ON HORSEBACK, IGNORED.` · `FRIARS ON FOOT, WITH NOTHING.` · `SENT TO STUDY, AND STUDY HARD.` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN PASS IT ON.` · then, large: `PREACH THE GOSPEL TO EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one idea well. Choose one thing you've heard many times and never really thought about. A line from the Creed. A verse. A word from this path. Hold just that one thing for the sit. Turn it over slowly. What does each word say? What does it leave out? What question would you ask, if someone wise were sitting next to you? Don't reach for a conclusion. Just stay with it. If you pray, you can let the study become prayer. The bell holds the time.
Dominic. He sold his books to feed the hungry, then founded the friars who study hard and preach, known as the Order of Preachers. Today's word.
Your line: to contemplate and to share. Today, take one good thing you've been thinking about, and hand it on to one person, simply. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: The universities
812.hook: Paris grew from its cathedral school; Oxford and Bologna rose in the same age
812.howItsDone: Catholic universities today, and the Church's own pontifical faculties, keep the medieval pairing of faith and study; Catholics speak of theology as faith seeking understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic, who sold his books for the hungry and then sent his friars to study. Your line was to contemplate and to share. What did you hand on? Day eight hundred twelve.

An open book on a coat of arms, the arms of the University of Oxford, and written across its pages, Dominus illuminatio mea. The words open a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" A place famous for lectures and libraries and examinations chose, for its badge, a line of prayer. It's a clue to where the whole idea came from. Today's word is the place that badge belongs to: the university.
screen: `DOMINUS ILLUMINATIO MEA.` → `A PSALM ON AN OPEN BOOK.` → `A CLUE TO WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: First, the cathedral. In the middle ages, bishops kept schools at their cathedrals to train clergy to read, to sing the liturgy and to understand scripture. In Paris, the school by the cathedral of Notre-Dame drew teachers, and the teachers drew students, until the streets around were full of both. Then, the guild. In the cities, bakers and masons banded together into guilds to protect their trade. Teachers and students did the same. In Latin, such a sworn body could be called a universitas, a whole company of people bound together. The masters of Paris, the students of Bologna and the scholars of Oxford organized this way, and won rights from popes and kings to govern themselves. Next, the method. A day at a medieval university was built on two things. The lecture: a master read a text aloud, line by line, and explained it. And the disputation: a question was posed, the arguments against were stated fairly, then the master gave his answer and replied to each objection. Some readers see Anselm's phrase from day eight hundred, faith seeking understanding, turned here into a daily routine. You didn't win by shouting. You had to state the other side fairly before you answered it. Last, what we inherited. Degrees, the lecture hall, the idea that a question deserves an argument: these grew in schools where theology was taught alongside law and medicine and the arts. The friars from yesterday's story went to these towns to study and teach. Learning was treated as a way of loving God with the mind. That's today's line: faith builds schools.
screen: `THE SCHOOL BY THE CATHEDRAL.` · `A GUILD OF MASTERS AND STUDENTS.` · `LECTURE, THEN DISPUTATION.` · `FAITH SEEKING UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn something difficult, the medieval way. Pick a question you've been avoiding because it's hard: in your faith, your work, your life. For the sit, do what a disputation does. First, say the strongest case against your own view, as fairly as you can. Then let your own answer come. Then see whether it can answer that objection. No need to finish. If you pray, you can begin with the psalm's own line: the Lord is my light. The bell holds the time.
University. The universitas: a sworn company of masters and students, growing in cities like Paris from the schools beside the cathedrals. Today's word.

Your line: faith builds schools. Look back at this week: stones at San Damiano, a crib, wounds, a song, a door, Dominic, and now a school. Today, learn one hard thing properly. Day eight hundred twelve.
